title: Four orders of existence and three modes of signification
en:
**On the words, “The third investigation: existence.”** Existence is spoken of in ordered ranks. Highest is **existence in external realities** (*al-aʿyān*), original or primary existence, in which the identity and reality of a thing obtain—or, more precisely, the very obtaining of that identity and reality. Next is **existence in minds**, a nonoriginal mode resembling the shadow of a body: what obtains through it is a representation corresponding to a thing, so that if the represented content existed externally it would be that thing, as a tree's shadow, were it to acquire bodily reality in the relevant way, would be the tree. Then come **existence in expression** and **existence in writing**. Relative to the thing itself, these last two are metaphorical: what exists when we say “Zayd” is the sound conventionally assigned to him, and what exists in the written word is a figure assigned to the sound that designates him. Neither is Zayd's essence nor a mental representation of his essence. But relative to the words and visible marks considered as things in their own right, the sound and the mark have genuine external existence.

In this ordering, a later member indicates what precedes it: mental existence signifies external existence; speech signifies the mental content; writing signifies speech. There are therefore three indications. The **first** is purely intellectual, unaffected by differences between people or linguistic conventions in either indicant or indicated: whichever language one uses for “sky,” the external thing is the same individual reality and the mental content is its determinate corresponding representation. The **other two** are established by convention. In the first, different communities may designate the same mental representation by different sounds—the Arabic *samāʾ*, the Persian equivalent, and so on—while the indicated content does not vary with the languages. In the second, both the written indicant and the spoken expression signified by it may vary. Variation in written form can arise even when the spoken expression remains the same, because different writing conventions represent it differently.

**Objection:** Indication means that apprehending one thing leads to apprehending another. If mental images indicate external things, and apprehension of external things just is the occurrence of their mental images, saying that mental images indicate external things seems equivalent to saying that the occurrence of mental images causes the occurrence of the same mental images. **Reply:** When a judgment is made about external things, the things present in mind are their images, but through those images the judgment concerns external reality. When we say “The world is originated,” what occurs in the mind is the representation of the world and of origination; through these we know origination to belong to the world as it exists externally.

**Further objection:** We are certain that speakers originally assigned words to the **external things they understand**, and intend them to designate those things. Even those who deny mental images acknowledge linguistic naming and signification. If an intelligible has no external existence, such as the nonexistent or impossible, only then—on the theory of mental images—is the image itself what the expression signifies. **Reply:** The present argument presupposes mental representations, whose acceptance is regarded as very close to what intellect finds immediately evident. On hearing a word a representation becomes inscribed in the soul; by it one knows a judgment of an external thing. The external reality is thus said to be indicated by the image, and the image by the word. The indication of speech by writing needs little explanation. It also economizes the effort of memory: one needs to preserve a manageable set of written shapes arranged in the order of letters, rather than a distinct graphic image for every individual meaning.

title: Arguments for mental existence
en:
**On the words, “It is argued.”** That knowledge, especially knowledge of what has no external realization, requires the establishment of something in the mind is evident, almost on the level of what is necessary. Some have consequently claimed that to deny mental existence is to deny a necessary truth. Its defenders advance several arguments.

**First:** We make affirmative judgments about things that have no external realization whatsoever: for example, that the conjunction of contradictories entails each of the contradictories, or is distinct from the conjunction of contraries. Affirmation is a judgment that something is established of something, and the establishment of a predicate for what is in no sense established is self-evidently impossible. Impossibles must therefore have some establishment if these judgments are to be valid; since it is not external, it is mental. Another formulation notes that some affirmative propositions have subjects which are not externally realized, whereas an affirmative proposition requires its subject to have existence in some sense. It must therefore exist in the mind. When one says that we ascribe “positive predicates” to impossibles, *positive* means *affirmative*. Thus the objection that the establishment is either external, which is impossible, or mental, which begs the question, misses the point. It is also possible to intend establishment in general; dividing it into external and mental does not force us at the outset to select one and so face either impossibility or begging the question.

**Second:** A universal is conceived, and whatever is conceived is established inasmuch as the intellect distinguishes it. Hence the universal is established. It is not externally established, because everything externally existent is individuated. It is therefore established in the mind.

**Third:** Some propositions are universal affirmatives taken as *real* propositions (*qaḍāyā ḥaqīqiyya*), and such propositions require their subjects to exist. Their subjects need not exist externally at all, as in “Every phoenix is an animal.” Even where instances exist externally, the scope of the proposition does not stop with those instances, as in “Every body is finite,” “Every body is originated,” or “Every body is composed of indivisible parts,” and many other claims used in the sciences. A judgment about all the relevant instances therefore requires considering mental existence. A passage in *al-Mawāqif* seems to classify “The impossible is nonexistent” as a real proposition, but it is not so classified in their technical usage.

**Objection:** We do not concede that affirmative predication entails that the subject exists. You say that one thing's being established of another depends upon that other's being established in itself. But affirmative predication need mean only that what the subject-expression is true of is what the predicate-expression is true of. It does not posit a further actuality of one thing in another; that is a mode of expression and already assumes mental existence. What is needed is merely that subject and predicate be distinguishable **for the intellect**, in the sense that they are conceived. Thus the three arguments reduce to: we apprehend and understand things without external existence, so they must be established in the mind, because understanding is the occurrence of the thing itself or its representation in the intellect. But that is the very issue under dispute: understanding as occurrence within the mind is precisely the position defended by proponents of mental existence. Otherwise knowledge of any thing would suffice to prove their thesis.

**Reply:** Even if one does not assume the theory of an image occurring in the mind, understanding, comprehending, and distinguishing something require a connection between knower and known. This holds whether knowledge is an image of the thing occurring in the intellect, a special relation between knower and known, or a quality accompanied by such a relation. A connection between a knower and sheer nothingness is necessarily impossible. The object understood therefore needs establishment in some sense. Universals and other nonexistents—and, especially, impossibles—cannot be established externally; their establishment must therefore be mental.

**Further objection to this reply:** Concepts lacking external existence need not exist *in the intellect*. They might be self-standing forms, as in Plato's separate Forms, to be discussed under quiddity, or the suspended forms affirmed by some philosophers. According to the latter, each existent has a counterpart in an imaginal realm which is neither intelligible nor sensible, discussed later at the end of the work. **Fourth alternative:** The forms might subsist in some separate intelligence, as philosophers say forms of generated things are inscribed in the Active Intellect. Perhaps this is what the Imām intended by forms or bodies absent from us; otherwise the inherence of nonexistents in bodies is unintelligible.

**Reply:** We are discussing nonexistents, above all impossibles. Such things cannot subsist by their own external identities; nor can their identities subsist in the Active Intellect, since an impossible thing has no individual identity to subsist. At most the Active Intellect could *conceive* them. Yet that account already entails the thesis, for conceiving would occur through a representation in the intellective knower. The representation would therefore be inscribed in an intellectual power, which is what mental existence means. If understanding follows one method, the understanding of existing things, too, occurs through their intellectual representations. The author of *al-Mawāqif* observes that if the forms in the Active Intellect are universal images and quiddities, the reality called mental existence is established, since the aim is some distinction of intelligibles other than their external distinction by individual identity, whether our intellect generates those forms or apprehends them elsewhere. This reply is itself open to criticism: it establishes that intelligibles are distinguishable to an intellect by their images and quiddities, but the question is precisely whether that happens **through images occurring in the mind itself**.

title: The deniers' objections: contradictory qualities and enormous objects in the mind
en:
**On the words, “The opponents maintained.”** Since the theory of mental existence rests on the claim that understanding requires a thing to occur in the intellect, opponents concentrate on rejecting that claim. **First:** If conceiving a thing entailed its presence in the intellect, conceiving heat and cold would make the mind both hot and cold, which is impossible because contraries would meet and because an intellect would possess properties of bodies. **Second:** On understanding the heavens, the immense heavens would have to fit within the intellect, or within the imagination when imagined; this is necessarily false. **Third:** On apprehending nonexistents, they would become externally existent, for they would exist within the intellect, which itself exists externally. Whatever exists in something that exists within another is existent within that latter: water in a jug inside a house exists in the house.

The answer to all three is that they fail to distinguish **primary or original external existence**, by which a thing has its individual external identity, from **nonoriginal mental existence**, by which the intellectual representation obtains. What is characterized by heat is what receives the individual external reality of heat, not its representation; and opposition exists between the identities of heat and cold, not between their intellectual images. What is necessarily too large to be contained in intellect or imagination is the individual, external reality of the heavens, not its universal or particular image. Something located within what is itself located within another is indeed also located within the latter *when both modes of being are original external existences* and the contents are individual entities—as with water, jug, and house. But a nonexistent's obtaining in a mind which itself exists externally is different: the nonexistent has an image whose presence is nonoriginal, whereas the mind has an external individual reality. In general, a thing's quiddity—its intellectual representation—differs from its external individuality in many concomitants. The former is universal and abstracted; the latter is not. The latter is the source of effects; the former is not. Their correspondence means that, if the intellectual quiddity were to exist in external reality, it would be that individual thing, and if the external thing were stripped of individuating accidents and extraneous concomitants, its quiddity would be the intellectual one. Thus it is no objection that if the intellectual image equalled the external one all the alleged impossibilities would follow, whereas if it did not equal it it would not be an image of that thing: correspondence here is not the identity of the modes of existing.

title: Four positions concerning the nonexistent and an intermediate state
en: **On the words, “The fourth investigation.”** There is a disagreement over whether a nonexistent is **established** (*thābit*) and a **thing** (*shayʾ*), and over whether there is an intermediate status between existent and nonexistent. The combinations are four: to affirm both claims, deny both, affirm the first but deny the second, or deny the first but affirm the second. A nonexistent can either be established or not, and in either case an intermediate status may or may not be admitted. The true position is the denial of both claims, on the basis that existence and establishment have equivalent meaning and nonexistence and negation likewise. As a negated thing is not established, a nonexistent is not established; and as nothing intervenes between what is established and what is negated, so nothing intervenes between existent and nonexistent. *Thingness* is coextensive with existence: every existent is a thing, and conversely. The term *coextensive* is used both when two terms are the same in concept (and are thus synonyms) and when they are merely equivalent in extension (with distinct concepts). Whether the concepts of existence and thingness are identical is disputed; indeed it may be denied because “Blackness exists” is informative whereas “Blackness is a thing” is not. The result is that anything that can be known is existent, established, and a thing if it obtains either externally or mentally; if not, it is nonexistent, negated, and no thing.

title: Affirming intermediate states: the Abū Hāshim theory of a ḥāl
en:
Some opponents deny that there is no intermediary. Among our theologians the Imām al-Ḥaramayn at an earlier stage and al-Qāḍī adopted this, and among the Muʿtazila, Abū Hāshim. They maintain: if what is known has no establishment—in the external world, since the present discussion assumes the denial of mental existence; otherwise anything known is plainly in the mind—then it is nonexistent. If it has establishment *independently and in respect of its own identity*, it is existent; if it has establishment only dependently upon another, it is a **state** (*ḥāl*). A state therefore falls between existent and nonexistent. It is a quality belonging to an existent which is neither existent nor nonexistent, such as *being-knowing* (*ʿālimiyya*) or *being-powerful* (*qādiriyya*). By “quality” they mean what cannot be known or reported of independently but only in dependence on something else; an essence, by contrast, can be known independently and is either existent or nonexistent. On this account, an existent means an essence possessing existence, and a nonexistent means an essence possessing nonexistence. A state does not itself possess such an essence, so is neither. Hence the restriction to “quality” rather than “essence.” The restriction to “a quality of an **existent**” excludes attributes of the nonexistent, which are nonexistent, not states; the phrase “not existent” excludes genuine existent properties such as blackness and whiteness; “nor nonexistent” excludes negative properties.

Al-Kātibī objects that this definition does not hold for the Muʿtazila, since they make *substantiality* (*jawhariyya*) a state of an essence both while it exists and while it does not. This objection works only if the claim is actually established from Abū Hāshim. Among the Muʿtazila some reject states altogether, and others affirm them but not in this precise manner. Al-Kātibī further reports Abū Hāshim as the first advocate of the doctrine of states. His more specific position was that accidents not conditioned on life—such as colour and odour—do not necessitate a state or quality in their receptive subjects, with the exception of spatial being (*kawn*), which necessitates the state of being located or occurring (*kāʾiniyya*). Accidents conditioned on life, on the other hand, produce states in their subjects: knowledge produces being-knowing and power produces being-powerful. Al-Qāḍī and the Imām al-Ḥaramayn maintain more generally that every positive property produces a state in its subject: spatial being produces being located, blackness produces being black, knowledge produces being-knowing, and so forth. These are positions being reported and distinguished, not all doctrines held by every Muʿtazilī.

title: Affirming the establishment of some nonexistents
en: Another group disputes the denial that the nonexistent is established. This is the position of most Muʿtazila as represented here. They say: whatever is known either has existence externally, and is then **existent**, or does not, and is **nonexistent**; there is no intermediate status between these. But under a different division, what is known either possesses self-establishment (*taḥaqquq fī nafsihi*, *taqarrur*) and is **established**, or lacks it and is **negated**. Everything externally existent is self-established, but not everything self-established exists externally. The class of existents is therefore narrower than the class of established things. Everything without self-establishment lacks external existence, but not everything lacking external existence lacks self-establishment. Thus the class of **negated** objects is narrower than the class of nonexistents: some nonexistents are not negated, but are established.

title: Combining established nonexistents with intermediate states
en:
A third group contests both denials. According to these Muʿtazilīs, what is known and externally obtains either does so independently, making it **existent**, or only through dependence on another, making it a **state**; what has no external occurrence is **nonexistent**. The nonexistent is, in turn, either established in itself or negated. Thus some nonexistents are established and an intermediate category between existent and nonexistent, the state, is admitted.

The wording might suggest that *established* is a subdivision of *nonexistent*. Properly it is not: the two classes overlap, because the established also includes existents and states, which are not nonexistents under the given division, while the nonexistent includes the negated, which is not established. If, however, the nonexistent and the negated are treated as disjoint, as stated in the summary of *al-Muḥaṣṣal* concerning those who maintain that the nonexistent is a thing and who say that the impossible is not *nonexistent* but *negated*, the division would be better expressed as follows. What is known and not established in itself is **negated**. What is established is, if it has external occurrence, either existent independently or a dependent state; if it has none, it is nonexistent. A third group contests both denials. title: The appeal to self-evidence against established nonexistents and intermediate states
en: **On the words, “Our position in both places.”** We appeal to necessary intellectual judgment against both the established thingness of nonexistents and an intermediary between existent and nonexistent. We understand by establishment only existence, whether in the intellect or in external reality, and by nonexistence the denial of such existence. Thingness is coextensive with being. Whatever is established in the intellect or externally is an existent in the relevant order, and just as there can be no intermediary between established and negated, neither can there be one between existent and nonexistent. The opponent, in al-Taftāzānī's judgment, is resisting what is evident. Making *existence* narrower than *establishment*, or *nonexistence* narrower than *negation*, and defining existent as an essence possessing the attribute of existence and nonexistent as one possessing nonexistence so that a quality may be placed between them, are at most terminological conventions about which there need be no dispute as conventions. What is challenged is the supposed reality corresponding to the distinctions.

title: Argument from divine power and the impossibility of an externally established nonexistent
en:
**On the words, “It is argued.”** Some in our school do not take the denial of an established nonexistent as self-evident and therefore argue for it. **First:** If the nonexistent were established, power could not affect anything among the possibles. The consequent is demonstrably false and rejected by agreement. The reason is that power would act either upon the essence itself, which on this supposition is eternal, and an eternal object cannot be produced by power; or upon its existence, which would count as a **state** (*ḥāl*), either as a consequence of the opponents' own principles or because evidence for the doctrine of states is said to be supplied later. Those who affirm states agree that states are not objects brought into being by power. It is necessary, for example, that blackness's being a colour and a knower's being-knowing through knowledge are not dependent upon the action of power. The different argument sometimes offered—that if the knower's being-knowing or the moving thing's being-in-motion were caused by an agent these could obtain without knowledge or motion, eliminating accidents—is weak.

One should further distinguish the eternal character of an **attribute's being possessed** from the eternity of the attribute itself. The claim that something is not an object of power does not make the *existence* itself eternal. Rather, it would make the essence's **being-qualified-by-existence** eternal, on the theory that qualification is a relation between essence and existence dependent upon neither beyond themselves. This is because the advocates allow establishment either without a cause or through a non-powerful cause.

**Reply:** The alternatives are incomplete. Power might produce the essence's **being-qualified by existence**. It cannot simply be said that qualification has no external standing. One argument for that says that, if qualification were established, its being established would require a further qualification, and so on endlessly. Another recalls that there is no external inherence between quiddity and existence analogous to whiteness in a body; their additionality is intellectual. Otherwise a nonexistent quiddity would be qualified by existence, because quiddity without existence would be externally nonexistent; quiddity considered as such exists only in thought. The response to the first argument is to deny that an infinite regress of **established things** is impossible in the same way that an infinite regress of existents is, even if one grants that establishment-of-qualification requires a further qualification. The response to the second is to deny that an **externally established but nonexistent** quiddity cannot acquire existence and become existent by it, as a nonblack body acquires blackness and becomes black. The impossible case arises only when the alleged subject has no establishment externally at all. This explains the Imām's claim that the doctrine of the established nonexistent arises out of the doctrine that existence is additional to quiddity: once they regarded the existence of blackness as an attribute additional to its quiddity, they thought the quiddity could remain without the attribute. They also thought that, if existence supervenes upon and inheres in a quiddity, that quiddity cannot be absolute negation; so it must be established before existence. The reasoning can equally be reversed: an essence externally established before existence cannot have an existence identical with itself, since its establishment and disappearance would then be those of existence itself.

title: Arguments from negation, independence, and infinitely many essences
en:
**Second:** The nonexistent is characterized by nonexistence. Nonexistence is a negative attribute, since it is the removal of existence, a positive attribute. A subject characterized by a negative property is negated, as one characterized by a positive property is established. **Reply:** If “negative property” means something which is pure negation in itself, so that possessing it means being negated, we deny that every nonexistent is characterized by such a property. That would follow only if nonexistence were equivalent to negation, whereas the opponents make it broader, since existence is narrower than establishment. If instead “negative property” means a qualification which negates one particular feature—for example, not occupying a place or not being originated—then possession of it does not imply that its subject is itself negated: the Necessary is described by many negative attributes. An existent can have privative properties just as, on the opponents' principles, a nonexistent can bear positive attributes.

**Third:** If essences are established in the state of nonexistence and, according to you, their establishment is not derived from another, they must be necessary. For to be necessary is precisely to be independent of another. Then possibles would be necessary, and Necessary Existents would be multiplied. An alternative formulation says that, if essences were established, their establishment would be either necessary—multiplying necessary beings—or possible, and therefore originated and preceded by negation. Essences as such would then be preceded by negation. Besides presupposing that every possibly established item is originated in the sense of being preceded by negation, this alternative does not refute essences' establishment **without existence**: it would show only that the establishment of those essences in nonexistence had earlier been absent. **Reply:** A Necessary Existent is independent of another in **existence**, not merely in *establishment*, which is taken to be broader.

**Fourth:** You say that the essences established in nonexistence are infinite in number, which is impossible. By agreement, the amount which has passed from them into existence is finite. The entire total would therefore exceed what remains in nonexistence by that finite amount, and so the total would be finite, since it exceeds something else by a finite amount. **Reply:** We deny that a quantity exceeding another by a finite amount must itself be finite. That follows only if the other quantity is finite. Here the essences remaining nonexistent are infinite just as the total is. **Further objection:** The remainder is surely fewer than the whole; by mapping the two sets element by element it must fall short and so be finite, with the same result for the whole. **Answer:** The argument is opposed by the succession of ranks of numbers; and difference in greater and lesser is denied when comparing two infinites. Even conceding the argument, proving that nonexistent essences are not infinite would not prove that they are not established.

title: Fifth argument: the extension of the term “nonexistent”
en:
**Fifth:** Nonexistent must be equal to, narrower than, or wider than *negated*; a total disjunction between them is excluded because they manifestly share some instances. If *nonexistent* is equal to or narrower than *negated*, every nonexistent is negated, and no negated thing is established: therefore no nonexistent is established. If instead nonexistent is broader, it cannot be pure negation—otherwise no difference between the general and the narrower class would remain—but must be something established. Yet it applies to what is negated. Hence negation itself would be established, because whatever falls under a positive property is established. That is impossible: one contradictory would be predicable of the other. This is the Imām's presentation, though he phrases it variously. In one formulation he compares *nonexistence* with *negation* and draws the syllogism: every negation is nonexistence; every nonexistence is established; therefore every negation is established—an impossibility.

**Reply:** We do not concede that whatever is not pure negation must be wholly positive. There can be a concept, *nonexistent*, some instances of which are established (possible nonexistents) and others negated (impossibles). This suffices to distinguish it from *negated*, and it remains false that every nonexistent is established. The negated therefore does not become established merely by falling under *nonexistent*.

The author of *al-Mawāqif* regards the argument instead as **ad hominem** against the opponent's principles. If the nonexistent were established, it would be broader than, and conceptually distinct from, the negated. Since the opponent says every distinguishable thing is established, the term *nonexistent* would be established; because it applies to the negated, the negated, too, would be established, since whatever falls under an established positive attribute is established. The previous reply would not address *this* formulation. But al-Taftāzānī remarks that the reply was advanced against the Imām's own argument, where the alleged ad hominem character makes no difference. If an ad hominem point is really intended, most premises are unnecessary: it would suffice to say that if nonexistent and negated were not the same, the negated would be distinct from the nonexistent and therefore established. Indeed, this has no special connection to the nonexistent's alleged establishment: one could simply say that if the negated differs from the existent, it is distinguishable from it and must be established. Why make the *narrower* extension of nonexistent imply its negation, while making its *wider* extension imply its establishment, when distinctness is available in either case?

**Further objection:** Given that the opponent already asserts the established status of the nonexistent, why struggle to establish that assertion before inferring that what is negated is established? Why not say straightaway that if the nonexistent is established and includes the negated, the latter is established? **Reply:** The opponent asserts that certain **possible nonexistent essences** are established. The argument tries to prove the establishment of the **unrestricted attribute or concept “nonexistent”**, from which the establishment of its bearers would then be inferred. This explains why the wording in *al-Mawāqif* repeats the noun *nonexistent*: the first instance refers to the subject or bearer, the second to the attribute. Otherwise “if the nonexistent is established, the nonexistent is established” would be empty. In the Imām's presentation, the word “broader” has to cover both absolute inclusion and partial overlap for the alternatives to be exhaustive; in the *Mawāqif* formulation it can be read as absolute inclusion, with the connection made by the term's application to every negated object.

title: The opponents' first two arguments for established possible nonexistents
en:
**On the words, “The opponents maintained.”** Those holding that a possible nonexistent is nevertheless externally established advance several arguments. **First:** It is distinguishable; whatever is distinguishable is established. It is distinguishable because a nonexistent can be **known** and hence distinct from an unknown, **willed** and distinct from what is not willed, or **within the scope of power** and distinct from what is not. The major premise is defended by saying that discrimination requires intellectual pointing—“this” and “that”—and pointing requires its referent to be established; one cannot point to sheer negation.

**Second:** A possible nonexistent is possible; every possible thing is established. Possibility, to be discussed later, is a positive attribute, and anything bearing a positive attribute must be established. **Reply to the first:** If distinction is alleged to require external establishment, we deny it; it would follow only if the distinction itself were external. If mental distinction is meant, the argument does not prove external establishment. **Reply to the second:** We deny that possibility is positive in the sense of an externally established quality. It is an intellectual consideration for which it suffices that its subject be established in the intellect.

Consider further that impossibles—the Necessary's partner, the conjunction of contradictories, or one body occupying two spatial regions in one instant—can be distinguished from each other and from existing things, yet they are undoubtedly negated. A mountain made of ruby or a sea of quicksilver can likewise be conceived as distinct and possible, although such imagined composites are not actually established, as all sides agree. Impossibles serve as an objection or counterexample to the first argument; the imagined composites to both arguments. One might also object by citing **states** of existence and similar attributes: they are distinct, yet according to the theory they are not established while nonexistent, for they are neither existent nor nonexistent, and a state belongs to an existent only. There is a difficulty with this last objection. The opponent's rule is simply that every distinguishable thing is externally established. If it is existent, it is established as an existent; if nonexistent, in nonexistence; and if neither existent nor nonexistent, it has its appropriate intermediate status. Existence and other states have no state of nonexistence at all; so how could their not being established **in nonexistence** refute the rule?

title: The colour black, essentiality, and the lexical meaning of shayʾ
en:
**Third:** To say that a possible nonexistent is externally established means, for example, that blackness which does not exist is nevertheless **blackness in itself**, whether or not other things exist. That seems plain: if blackness were blackness through another, the removal of that other would abolish blackness's being blackness. The consequent is impossible, for then a blackness which exists would cease to be blackness when the thing that makes it blackness disappeared. **Reply:** The consequence is denied. It would follow only if blackness's **existence** persisted while whatever makes it blackness had disappeared. Why cannot the removal of the other also remove the existence of blackness, if it is the cause of that existence or inseparably accompanies its cause?

**Objection:** If blackness's being blackness disappeared with that other, blackness would not be blackness, something self-evidently impossible. **Reply:** If this means simply the **negative predication** that nonexistent blackness is not blackness, its impossibility is denied. If it means an **infinite or privative predication**—an independently established blackness which is nonblack—we deny that it follows: it would follow only if the blackness were still independently established in itself. **Further objection:** Every thing has a quiddity by which it is what it is, without regard for anything else, whether essential concomitant or separable accident. Therefore blackness must be blackness whether or not anything else exists. **Reply:** The principle entails only that blackness is blackness **whether or not something else is being considered**; it does not entail that it remains blackness **when something else is absent**. Abstracting from another thing is not the same as negating its existence. In the same way one may say a thing is existent without considering its cause, but not when that cause does not exist.

**On the words, “This concerns thingness.”** The foregoing dispute and proofs concern the thingness of a nonexistent **as external establishment**. Whether the *word* “thing” (*shayʾ*) applies to such a nonexistent *properly* is a linguistic question settled by transmitted usage and linguistic evidence. Disagreement has arisen because expressions are used in various contexts. In our view, *shayʾ* properly designates an existent, as its widespread usage suggests. There is no denial that it may also be used of a nonexistent figuratively, as in the Qurʾānic phrase “Our word to a thing when We will it is merely to say to it ‘Be!’ and it is” (16:40), or “I created you before, when you were not a thing” (19:9); such instances do not settle proper rather than figurative usage. The position attributed to Abū al-Ḥusayn al-Baṣrī and al-Naṣībī—that it is literal of the existent and figurative of the nonexistent—is precisely our own. Many Muʿtazila call it a term for whatever is **known**, apparently implying that an impossible is a thing, which they usually deny. They could reply either by denying that an impossible is known, to be discussed later, or by denying that they exclude calling it a thing. Al-Zamakhsharī indeed states that it names whatever can be known, encompassing existent and nonexistent, possible and impossible; what he denies is the impossible's being a *thing* in the sense of external establishment. Others use it for what is **not impossible**, whether existent or nonexistent. The reports that Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Nāshiʾ restricted it to the eternal, the Jahmiyya to the originated, or Hishām ibn al-Ḥakam to body, are very implausible—not simply because the term is also used of other objects, for each might claim those usages figurative, as we do regarding 16:40—but because such restrictions lack support from linguistic testimony or even a plausible ground. As ordinary word-usage favours literal rather than figurative meaning, all parties must finally appeal to transmitted linguistic evidence, dominant usage, the immediate understanding of competent speakers, or similar criteria.

The position attributed to Abū al-Ḥusayn al-Baṣrī and al-Naṣībī—that it is literal of the existent and figurative of the nonexistent—is precisely our own. Many Muʿtazila call it a term for whatever is known, apparently implying that an impossible is a thing, which they usually deny. They could reply either by denying that an impossible is known, to be discussed later, or by denying that they exclude calling it a thing. Al-Zamakhsharī indeed states that it names whatever can be known, encompassing existent and nonexistent, possible and impossible; what he denies is the impossible's being a thing in the sense of external establishment. Others use it for what is not impossible, whether existent or nonexistent. The reports that Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Nāshiʾ restricted it to the eternal, the Jahmiyya to the originated, or Hishām ibn al-Ḥakam to body, are very implausible—not simply because the term is also used of other objects, for each might claim those usages figurative, as we do regarding 16:40—but because such restrictions lack support from linguistic testimony or even a plausible ground. title: The first proof of intermediate states: existence itself
en:
**On the words, “Those affirming the state argued in several ways.”** Their **first** argument is that existence is not an existent. If it were, it would need its own existence, and that existence a further existence, yielding an infinite regress. Nor is it a nonexistent, for then it would be described by its contradictory—that is, by something to which the negation of existence applies. On the supposition of a middle status, *nonexistence* is not the contradictory of *existence*, but a narrower class: the contradictory is *not-existence*. Thus existence itself exemplifies what is neither existent nor nonexistent.

The author of *al-Tajrīd* replies that existence is not subject to the division into existent and nonexistent, so it falls under neither. But that simply grants what is to be established and admits a middle. **Objection:** An intermediary ought to be a subdivision of what is established; existence, however, is not something established any more than it is negated, for it is *establishment* itself. Just as neither establishment nor negation is itself established or negated, this does not establish something intermediate between them. **Reply:** The remedy worsens the illness, since this restates the very claim of an intermediate between established and negated, where the two contradictories are supposed jointly exhaustive.

The Imām replies instead that existence **is existent**, and its existence is itself, not something additional requiring a regress. It differs from other existents by a negative qualification: it has no quiddity other than existence. Another reply accepts that existence is **nonexistent** but denies that this characterizes it by its contradictory. Contradictory predication is impossible when a predicate is applied directly to its subject, as in “existence is nonexistence,” or “an existent is a nonexistent.” But with a **derived** predicate indicating the possession of a feature, as in “existence has nonexistence,” the impossibility is not conceded. Saying that an animal has what is *nonanimal*—blackness or whiteness, for example, among the accidents subsisting in it—is not thereby contradictory.

The nearer account is to distinguish unrestricted and particular existence. If *unrestricted existence* is meant, it is not an externally existent item. If *particular existence* is meant—such as the existence of the Necessary or of a human—it is existent, and the existence predicated of it is additional as an intellectually attributed universal or share thereof. No further existence is needed to produce a regress. If saying that existence “exists by an existence which is itself” means this, the expression is valid. If it means that existence is itself an existence while still lacking the possession of existence, the alleged intermediary between nonexistent and existent in the sense of **possessing existence** has not been removed. Al-Taftāzānī concludes that the difficulty in this argument is substantial.

title: The second proof: universals, genera, and alleged accidents inhering in accidents
en:
Their **second** argument concerns a universal which has actually existent particulars, as *human* does. The universal cannot be existent, since if it were externally existent it would be individuated and no longer universal. Nor can it be nonexistent, since a universal is a constituent of actually existing particulars such as Zayd, and the existent cannot have a nonexistent constituent. Similarly the genus *animal* is not existent because it is universal, nor nonexistent because it is part of the real essence of *human*. A genus of actual accidental quiddities—such as *colouredness* belonging to blackness—cannot be nonexistent for the same reason, nor existent, it is argued, because this would make one accident inhere in another. This alleged inherence is variously described: colour inhering in blackness because the genus is predicated of the species; blackness inhering in colour because the genus constitutes the species; colour inhering in the differentia “contracting vision,” for instance, because it is predicated of the differentia; or the differentia inhering in colour because the differentia constitutes the genus into a determinate species.

All these alternatives fail. A **part of a composite**, especially one predicable of the whole, is not for that reason an accident inhering in it, nor vice versa. Similarly the more general predicate and a qualification predicated of its subject need not be accidents inhering in it; indeed an external accident cannot be predicated **directly** of the subject in which it inheres, but only through a derived expression. Nor does a thing's being **constitutive** of another, whether by entering into its essential structure as genus enters into species or by determining it as differentia determines a genus, mean that one is an externally inhering accident of the other. Animal, for example, is predicated of human and is predicated of rational, though the rational differentia lies outside the genus *animal* as such and nevertheless determines it to an essence. The error arises from equivocating upon *accidental occurrence*, *predication*, and *subsistence in a subject*. The concise text alludes to this by saying that such subsistence has nothing to do with an accident's inhering in its substrate. It does not challenge the asserted impossibility of one accident externally inhering in another; perhaps that impossibility is separately established or is being conceded for the argument's sake.

There is, however, a stronger analysis which entirely removes the difficulty. In external reality there are not two independently identifiable components, **universal and individuation**, from which Zayd is formed; nor **genus and differentia**, from which a species is formed. There is no externally existing thing called universal human and another called Zayd's individuating character which compose a third thing, Zayd; likewise no external item *colour*, another item *contracting vision*, and a third thing made out of them, *blackness*. Hence it does not follow, by any of the accounts suggested above, that an accident inheres in another accident. Externally there is one reality; distinction and composition occur only according to the intellect. From this it follows only that the universal and genus have **mental existence**, in which there is no impossibility. It is astonishing that advocates of states suppose that a part of an existent must fall under the class of **not-existent**, the true contradictory of existent, but cannot fall under the class of **nonexistent**, which according to their own theory is merely a narrower class, not the contradictory of existent.

**On the words, “And ignorance follows only…”** The Imām objects to the account that genus and differentia are distinct only in the intellect. If the intellect's judgment corresponds to what is external, the advocates of states recover their thesis; if it does not, the judgment is ignorance and worthless. The initial reply is that the issue concerns **conceiving** genera and differentiae, which is not an affirmative judgment about external composition to be true or false. Ignorance would arise only if one judged that they were externally distinct when they were not. The Imām's intended objection is then restated: if the **representations or images** correspond to external things, the difficulty returns; if not, they are mistaken. The answer distinguishes two meanings of correspondence. If each intellectual representation must have a **separate external individual identity** corresponding to it, we deny that failure of such one-to-one correspondence is ignorance; it would be ignorance only if the representations purported to depict externally separate identities. If correspondence means that the external realization of what a representation conceives would be the very identity represented, and the intellectual understanding of that external identity yields these representations, then this does not require several externally distinct items. The intellect can abstract different representations from one reality under different considerations, as will be explained in the treatment of quiddity.

title: Counterargument from the states themselves
en:
**On the words, “The two arguments were countered by the state.”** The first counterargument is as follows. If **states** are established, they share establishment while differing in their particular features. The ground of agreement therefore differs from the ground of distinction; establishment must be additional to them. Yet their establishment is not negated, and so itself is established. The same infinite regress follows which the defenders of states alleged for existence. The second counterargument is that a state can be a universal predicable of established particulars. If established, the universal would be individuated; if negated, it could not be a constituent of what is established. The same reasoning holds if it is a genus of species. If it is a genus of accidents, the alleged accident-in-an-accident problem follows from their own premises. Their reply to these objections can therefore be made on behalf of those they oppose.

**Objection:** States do not admit agreement and difference, since those are properties of existent things. There is no common constituent and differentiating constituent for states requiring a further addition of establishment and consequent regress. Nor is there a determinate state corresponding to universality and another to particularity, or one to being-a-state and another to being-a-subject-of-a-state, from which the difficulty could arise. Existents, by the opponent's own admission, do admit such distinctions. Furthermore, infinite regress among **established states** has not been proved impossible; the proofs exclude regress among existent things. **Reply:** States necessarily admit conceptual agreement and difference: if what is understood by one is what is understood by another, they agree, and if not, they differ. Saying that agreement and difference are themselves states or qualities occurring only in existent subjects does not help: a quality can belong to what is established but not existent, and it is disputed that such agreement and difference are themselves *existent* states or qualities. At least some arguments to be presented against infinite regress also apply to established items. The Imām's further assertion that admitting such a regress would prevent us from disproving an infinite regress of past occurrences or establishing an eternal Maker is weak: the speaker is not conceding regress among **existents**, and the proof of the Maker need rule out only that latter regress.

The advocates reformulate the objection: states differ in their particular characters but share the general character of *being-a-state*; a common feature differs from the particularizing feature; thus a state requires another state, indefinitely. The Imām replies that being-a-state is not a positive property requiring a further state. A state simply means what is neither existent nor nonexistent—a negative designation. Sharing it is not sharing an additional state. The critical philosopher replies that, on their own doctrine, a state is not sheer negation but a **positive characterization of an existent** which is itself neither existent nor nonexistent. Otherwise the impossible would qualify as a state too, simply because it is not an existent or nonexistent in their specialized senses. There is a feature beyond the negations of existence and nonexistence that belongs to the things they call states and is shared by them. The state is not, however, said by them to admit sameness and difference, since, in their particular definition, two things are alike if they are **independent essences** understood in the same way, unlike if they are such essences understood differently; and a state is not an independent essence, because it cannot be understood by itself. Nor is the shared feature independently apprehended, so that one could judge its apprehended character to be identical with or different from that of another. The different responses must be kept apart, since they use distinct senses of “alike,” “different,” “established,” and “state.”

title: The third proof from bringing-into-existence
en:
**On the words, “The third.”** The third argument for an intermediate state is that **bringing-into-existence** (*ījād*) is not an existent. If it were, it would need to be brought into existence, and that producing would need another producing, and so indefinitely. But it is not nonexistent either: if producing something were nonexistent, the agent would not genuinely be a producer. No feature would have been gained when the effect issued from it; just as the agent did not count as producing before the issuance, it would not do so afterward. Nor can one say that the bringing-into-existence of bringing-into-existence is just the same thing: according to the opponent's own account of existent properties, bringing the effect into existence and bringing the predicate of production into existence are distinct matters.

**Reply:** We accept that *ījād* is externally nonexistent but deny that the agent thereby fails to be a producer. A true **affirmative predication** does not require the abstract feature from which the predicate is derived to exist externally. “Zayd is blind in external reality” and “The concurrence of contraries is impossible in external reality” can be true, although neither blindness nor impossibility is a separately externally existing feature. The argument therefore fails unless external existence of the abstract *ījād* is independently proved.

title: Consequences attributed to the doctrines of thingness and states
en:
**On the words, “They have further consequences.”** Those holding that nonexistents are things and that states are established develop further consequences from the two principles. They agree, according to the account given here, that there are **infinitely many essences established in nonexistence of each species**, and that a cause does not act upon those essences themselves, since they are established without a cause; the effect of causation is only their transition from nonexistence to existence. They also hold that the established essences do not differ in what it means to be an **essence**: they agree in the bare character of being an essence and differ through qualities rather than through the reality supposedly common to them. Were the essences absolutely equal in all respects, whatever is possible for one would be possible for another, which is plainly false. The individuals of a single species are, however, equal in their specific reality, as ordinarily acknowledged.

It is also reported as a consequence that one could be certain that the world has a Maker characterized by knowledge, power, and life, while still doubting that this Maker **exists**, until an argument for His existence is supplied. The doctrine permits positive attributes to belong to an established nonexistent. **Objection:** This would allow one to doubt that bodies exist even after knowing that they are moving or at rest, since they, too, could be so characterized in nonexistence and their existence would need separate proof—an extreme confusion. Some replies explain that we could **conceive** a Maker bearing these perfections and judge that any Maker would have to possess them, while still doubting whether there actually is a Maker. Or one could know conditionally that anything which, if existing, would make the world would, if existing, possess these attributes, without knowing that such a thing exists. But these replies have no special connection to the doctrine that nonexistents are externally established; they are equally available to its opponents. We reason to the Necessary's existence precisely because we can consider the concept of something necessary of existence and nevertheless need a proof that a corresponding reality exists. Similarly we can certainly judge a partner to God impossible: the putative essence different from God but endowed with existence and the other perfections cannot exist externally. Although writers present the consequence as generally agreed among advocates of the doctrine, it holds in the intended strong form only for those who assign positive qualifications to nonexistents.

title: Differences among advocates concerning nonexisting essences
en:
**On the words, “They differ.”** Another consequence of asserting the thingness of nonexistents is disagreement about which properties essences possess when nonexistent. Do nonexistent essences retain their **generic attributes**—substantiality in substance, blackness in blackness, and so on—and the properties dependent on these, such as inherence in a subject dependent upon blackness?

The majority, as represented here, answer yes. They reason that the essences agree in bare essentiality, so unless they differ through qualities they would all be one; that if they agree while nonexistent they must agree when existent, since what is essential cannot be lost through an accident, whereas if they differ their difference must be through qualities, since they share essentiality; and that the spatial occupation characteristic of substance when existent cannot follow simply from being an essence or being existent, since then it would belong equally to accidents. It must therefore depend upon a feature which the essence has even while nonexistent. **Reply:** Agreement in the broad concept of essentiality does not preclude real difference, just as realities may share the concept of existence without sharing their essences. If that is granted, the arguments do not establish their conclusion.

Abū Isḥāq ibn ʿAyyāsh holds instead that nonexisting essences lack all attributes. Since they all agree in essentiality, the allocation of one specific property to one of them cannot follow from that bare essentiality; nor from another property, since that would regress. It must follow from a separate cause. The cause cannot necessitate the property, because the cause has the same relation to all the essences; it must be a voluntary chooser. But an action of a voluntary agent is originated, so the nonexistent essence would be a subject for successive accidents, which both sides deny. The possession of particular qualities must therefore occur only upon existence. The answer is that the particular property might belong to the **particular essence in itself**, rather than to essentiality without qualification. The disagreement depends on confusion between the unrestricted predicate *essence* and the distinct essences which are its subjects.

Another disagreement concerns whether **spatial occupation** (*taḥayyuz*) differs from **substantiality** (*jawhariyya*). The majority call substantiality a property belonging to substance both while it exists and while it does not. Spatial occupation—the substance's requiring some spatial locus—is a property consequent upon the existent substance, or arising from substance on the condition of origination. It is called *kawn*. The substance's being in a **particular** locus is called *kāʾiniyya* and is explained through the prior spatial feature. Al-Shaḥḥām, al-Baṣrī, and Ibn ʿAyyāsh instead identify substantiality with spatial occupation, since they understand substance as what occupies a locus through itself.

They also dispute whether **being-nonexistent** (*maʿdūmiyya*) is a positive state belonging to nonexistents while nonexistent. Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Baṣrī affirms this; others deny it. Since that property would depend upon an essence it would be possible. If its cause were the essence itself or an involuntary necessitating cause, it would persist and the essence could never exist. If its cause were an agent acting through choice, directly or indirectly, it would be an originated state, which is held impossible in the context under discussion. Yet another disagreement asks whether nonexisting substances are **bodies** while nonexistent. The majority deny this; Abū al-Ḥusayn al-Khayyāṭ affirms it.

Do nonexistent essences retain their generic attributes—substantiality in substance, blackness in blackness, and so on—and the properties dependent on these, such as inherence in a subject dependent upon blackness?

The majority, as represented here, answer yes. They reason that the essences agree in bare essentiality, so unless they differ through qualities they would all be one; that if they agree while nonexistent they must agree when existent, since what is essential cannot be lost through an accident, whereas if they differ their difference must be through qualities, since they share essentiality; and that the spatial occupation characteristic of substance when existent cannot follow simply from being an essence or being existent, since then it would belong equally to accidents. It must therefore depend upon a feature which the essence has even while nonexistent. Reply: Agreement in the broad concept of essentiality does not preclude real difference, just as realities may share the concept of existence without sharing their essences. If that is granted, the arguments do not establish their conclusion.

Abū Isḥāq ibn ʿAyyāsh holds instead that nonexisting essences lack all attributes. Since they all agree in essentiality, the allocation of one specific property to one of them cannot follow from that bare essentiality; nor from another property, since that would regress. It must follow from a separate cause. The cause cannot necessitate the property, because the cause has the same relation to all the essences; it must be a voluntary chooser. But an action of a voluntary agent is originated, so the nonexistent essence would be a subject for successive accidents, which both sides deny. The possession of particular qualities must therefore occur only upon existence. The answer is that the particular property might belong to the particular essence in itself, rather than to essentiality without qualification. The disagreement depends on confusion between the unrestricted predicate essence and the distinct essences which are its subjects.

Another disagreement concerns whether spatial occupation (taḥayyuz) differs from substantiality (jawhariyya). The majority call substantiality a property belonging to substance both while it exists and while it does not. Spatial occupation—the substance's requiring some spatial locus—is a property consequent upon the existent substance, or arising from substance on the condition of origination. It is called kawn. The substance's being in a particular locus is called kāʾiniyya and is explained through the prior spatial feature. Al-Shaḥḥām, al-Baṣrī, and Ibn ʿAyyāsh instead identify substantiality with spatial occupation, since they understand substance as what occupies a locus through itself.

They also dispute whether being-nonexistent (maʿdūmiyya) is a positive state belonging to nonexistents while nonexistent. Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Baṣrī affirms this; others deny it. Since that property would depend upon an essence it would be possible. If its cause were the essence itself or an involuntary necessitating cause, it would persist and the essence could never exist. If its cause were an agent acting through choice, directly or indirectly, it would be an originated state, which is held impossible in the context under discussion. Yet another disagreement asks whether nonexisting substances are bodies while nonexistent. The majority deny this; Abū al-Ḥusayn al-Khayyāṭ affirms it.

title: Further subdivisions of states
en:
**On the words, “And like the division of the state.”** Among the consequences of affirming states is their division into a state **explained through an existent property of the essence**, as being-knowing is explained through knowledge and being-powerful through power, and a state not so explained, such as blackness's being-a-colour, which does not depend upon a further property residing in blackness; the same is said of existence's being existence. Another consequence is explaining differences among nonexisting essences through states. The proponents who say that essences differ by attributes call those attributes *states*. This also shows that, in these formulations, a state need not always be a quality of something **existent**.

Further distinctions are made among attributes of substances: some belong to the **whole**, the total organized structure composed of the constituent parts, such as being alive; some depend upon that structure, such as knowledge and power; others belong to the **several constituent individuals**, such as substantiality, existence, spatial being (*kawn*), and occupation of a particular place (*kāʾiniyya*). For accidents there is an essential property, such as blackness's being black; a property produced by an agent, such as existence; and one which follows the accident on the condition of its existence, such as inherence in a substrate. These are reports of the ramifications of the doctrine of states, not editorial endorsements of its ontology.

title: Why otherwise careful scholars adopted the disputed positions
en:
**On the words, “If you say.”** Since the externally established status of nonexistents and a middle between existent and nonexistent appear clearly, indeed necessarily, false, yet many distinguished investigators have nevertheless affirmed them—especially the intermediate state—the text identifies considerations which could have produced the illusion of truth in both cases.

**As to the first:** the intellect judges decisively that *blackness is blackness* in reality even if the causes required for its existence, agent and receptive subject, are absent. The causes of quiddity differ from the causes of existence, as will be explained. Those thinkers expressed this stable intelligibility by saying that the quiddity is “established externally,” because they discerned in it a sort of determinacy or truth independent of whether the causes of actual existence obtain. This was especially tempting to those who denied mental existence. It resembles the philosophers' claim that quiddities are not produced by an agent's act of making them what they are. In effect, they distinguished impossibles from possible nonexistents, which have determinate quiddities that at one time may be qualified by existence and at another not, according to whether the causes of existence are present. They called this determinacy “thingness” or “external establishment.”

**As to the second:** they considered certain things attributed to existents, such as a human's existence, God's act of bringing the human into being, Zayd's being-knowing, and blackness's being a colour. Arguments seemed to show that none was itself an externally existent thing, but they also saw no way to say that these had no truth whatever, because existents are described by them independently of the intellect's choosing to consider them. Furthermore, in their denial of mental existence, even supposing that the intellect considered such meanings would not establish them *in the intellect*. They therefore judged that such meanings have some external reality while being neither existent nor nonexistent: the intermediary they named *state*. Whenever an effect issues from its cause, it seems that both acquire a status absent before production—being-a-producer in the cause and existence in the effect. These cannot simply remain nonexistent, since there is an intelligible difference between the two occasions. Yet an argument seems to show that they are not independently existent; hence an intermediary appears to be required. This is an explanatory reconstruction of the temptation to the position, not al-Taftāzānī's endorsement of it.

title: Criticism of the explanation offered in al-Mawāqif
en:
**On the words, “As for building that upon…”** The author of *al-Mawāqif*, according to the wording of the textual archetype consulted here, professes a conjecture nearly approaching certainty about the foundation of the theory of intermediate states. Its proponents observed concepts which could **receive existence**, and called their obtaining *existence* and their absence *nonexistence*. They also observed concepts which cannot receive existence at all—intellectual considerations called **second intelligibles** by philosophers—and therefore said these are neither existent nor nonexistent, meaning they neither obtain nor can obtain in that way. On this interpretation, existence and nonexistence are contradictory **affirmation and negation** for us, but for them related as **possession and privation**. Yet this conjecture does not establish the truth.

**First**, it works only if the *nonexistent* is wholly disjoint from the *impossible* and never applied to it, as stated by the author of the abridgment, rather than being broader than *impossible* as the author of *al-Mawāqif* and others elsewhere explain: an impossible plainly cannot receive existence. **Second**, on the proposed analysis the state would be farther from existence than the nonexistent, since it neither obtains nor can obtain. Their own doctrine instead makes it surpass the nonexistent in determinacy, establishment, and truth, though falling short of an existent, even allowing a state to constitute part of an existent, as when being-a-colour is a constituent of blackness. **Third**, the conjecture contradicts the *Mawāqif* definition itself: a state is a known item which obtains **in dependence upon another rather than through its own independent essence**, or exists in the external realm **dependently, not independently**. The latter two objections can perhaps be answered by interpreting the possible “obtaining” of a nonexistent, but not a state, as **independent obtaining**, while granting that the state is closer to existence by having **dependent obtaining already**. The analysis must accordingly distinguish original external realization, dependent predicative obtaining, and sheer negation instead of speaking of “being” without qualification.

title: Fifth investigation: are nonexistences distinguishable?
en:
**On the words, “The fifth investigation.”** There is a famous disagreement concerning the distinctness of nonexistences (*tamāyuz al-aʿdām*). If the claim that they cannot differ means that distinction is not a separate external entity or that nonexistences lack several externally distinct individual identities, it is necessary and admits no dispute. If it means that the concept of nonexistence has no distinguishable intellectual instances to which different judgments hold true *in reality itself*, the claim is false. The absence of a cause necessitates the absence of its effect, but not conversely. The absence of a condition excludes the existence of what is conditioned by it, whereas the absence of the conditioned thing does not exclude the condition's existing. The absence of one contrary from a subject allows its opposite to supervene in that subject, unlike the absence of something which is not its contrary. Such differences are genuine even though their subjects are absences.

Since these distinctions are made in intellection, and there is disagreement over whether intellection itself constitutes mental existence, the author of *al-Mawāqif* presents the distinction of nonexistences as dependent upon that debate. He reports that those affirming mental existence would **deny** the distinction of nonexistences: all discriminated items, being thought, would have mental existence, so none would count as absolutely nonexistent without any trace of existence. Distinction would therefore apply only to existents. Those denying mental existence, he suggests, could **affirm** distinct nonexistences because they are conceived as distinct without acquiring any existence through being conceived. The historical state of opinion is actually the reverse, al-Taftāzānī observes. Philosophers who affirm mental existence also affirm the discrimination of absences, while the majority of theologians denying mental existence say that absences are not distinct. A better account of the dependency is this: if distinction is regarded as a positive characterization requiring the subject to be established, those who affirm mental existence can allow absences to differ **as conceived**, because they acquire mental establishment even while being nonexistences in themselves; those denying mental existence infer that absences cannot differ because they lack establishment altogether.

title: The absence of absence, unknowable subjects, and the restriction of judgment
en:
**On the words, “And nonexistence can be predicated of itself.”** Saying that absences differ in intellectual conception invites the objection that what differs is then the **mentally existing representation**, not nonexistence in itself. The text therefore highlights ways in which a thing may be an absence in itself but exist from the standpoint of being conceived. For example, **nonexistence can itself undergo nonexistence**: one conceives unrestricted nonexistence, the negation of external being, and the conception then passes from the mind. The absence of that representation is an absence of something which is an absence in itself, although it was existent insofar as it had an intellectual representation. Again, the disappearance of nonexistence from the mind is an instance of **nonexistence without qualification** in respect of its object, yet opposed to nonexistence when considered as the negation of it.

A further case concerns the **absolutely nonexistent**, meaning what is neither externally established nor represented intellectually. It can be made the subject of the judgment “Judgment concerning it is impossible” *insofar as it is conceived*, but is the counterpart of an established thing and cannot be judged about *insofar as it is altogether nonexistent*. A familiar objection says: something wholly unestablished cannot be made a subject of any judgment; judging that it cannot be judged is itself a judgment, and so is contradictory. **Reply:** It can be judged of from the standpoint of its **conceptual establishment in the intellect**; judgment concerning it is impossible from the standpoint of the meaning *wholly unestablished in itself*. The subjects differ by consideration, so the statements are not contradictory.

This also solves the celebrated difficulty raised against the principle that judgment concerning a thing requires its conception in some way. If that principle is sound, one might say that no thing lacking the requisite conception—an **utterly unknown** thing—can be judged about, since absence of a condition entails absence of what is conditioned. But the negative universal itself seems impossible. If the subject is known at all, it can in principle be judged about, making the universal statement “it cannot be judged about” false. If the subject is utterly unknown, the negative judgment about its incapacity for judgment is nevertheless a judgment, which is self-defeating. A proposed response makes the proposition conditional: it cannot be judged about **while** it remains utterly unknown. Yet the objection can be renewed by making the antecedent permanent: something always unknown cannot ever be judged about. Or we may reason that if judgment requires conception, it requires at least the **possibility** of conception; it would follow that one cannot even possibly judge about what is intrinsically inconceivable, yet to judge it impossible to judge is itself a judgment.

The same puzzle appears in many other statements: “*Ḍaraba* (‘he struck’) is a past-tense verb,” “*min* (‘from’) is a preposition and not a noun,” and “What cannot be conceived at all is not a universal.” We need a reply which addresses the shared source of the error. In each case the supposed subject changes with its mode of consideration. What is utterly unknown in itself cannot be judged of; but **the concept of the utterly unknown** is conceived and can be a subject of judgment. The word *ḍaraba*, with respect to what it signifies and its grammatical function, is a verb; **as the word “ḍaraba” mentioned in a metalinguistic statement**, it functions as a nominal subject. No contradiction follows.

Another attempted refutation of “no utterly unknown thing can be judged of” says that every utterly unknown thing either is a thing or is not a thing, either possible or not possible, and so either B or not-B, since contradictories cannot both fail. The difficulty is that neither disjunct may be **predicated in a judgment without first conceiving the subject**. We need not concede that either judgment, formed with an utterly unknown subject, is true or false as formulated; the elimination of contradictories would follow only if they were both negated **of one and the same appropriately conceived subject**. Here no affirmation or negation can properly be made. This is why the stronger discussion uses the dilemma about the subject's conception rather than the mere assertion of excluded middle.

title: The intellect's freedom to form negative and second-order concepts
en:
**On the words, “In general, there is no prohibition.”** This broadens the permission accorded to the intellect's operations and considerations. It may consider two contradictories as simple notions, for example *existent* and *not-existent*, or as propositions, “This exists” and “This does not exist,” and judge them contradictory: their two terms cannot truly apply together to the same thing, and their contradictory propositions cannot both be true in reality itself. Both are nevertheless **present in the intellect**, even when one expresses precisely something which lacks all existence in its own meaning. The intellect may even conceive the absence of everything, including its own absence. Conceiving the intellect's nonexistence presupposes that the intellect exists, so it apparently combines its existence and nonexistence—but the former is in the act of conceiving and the latter in the content conceived.

Likewise one may divide existent things into what is established in the intellect and what is **not established in the intellect**. The latter is the counterpart of the former with respect to its content, yet falls under the former insofar as it is **conceived**. The same applies to dividing objects into what can be conceived and what **cannot** be conceived: the second is itself conceived under the description “inconceivable,” and thus falls among the things conceivable as objects of that description. The intellect may discriminate the mentally established from the mentally unestablished, and conceivable from inconceivable, even though discrimination in thought requires two mental objects. In each case the negative member lacks an intellectual identity **as defined**, while it has an intellectual identity **as the representation formed for purposes of the present distinction**. The intellect can similarly form the notions of identity and nonidentity and discriminate them. Nonidentity is opposite to identity in what it means, yet can become an item of intellectual consideration. None of this is contradictory because different considerations are involved. These principles will help resolve numerous sophisms.
