title: Individuation: whether it is a real additional constituent (source I.108–111)
en:
**On the third chapter, concerning the concomitants of existence and quiddity.** The author of the *Tajrīd* places necessity, possibility, impossibility, eternity, and origination in the chapter on existence; individuation and unity and plurality in the chapter on quiddity; and cause and effect in a chapter of their own. The author of *al-Mawāqif* treats individuation under quiddity, necessity and its two opposites under a separate heading, unity and plurality under another, and cause and effect under yet another, placing eternity and origination alongside necessity and its opposites. The author of *al-Ṣaḥāʾif* treats necessity and its opposites and cause and effect as concomitants of **the existent**, while the rest are concomitants of **existence**. We have said generally that all are concomitants of existence and quiddity so that the heading remains appropriate on every arrangement.

**First investigation.** The individuation (*taʿayyun*) or particularization (*tashakhkhuṣ*) whereby a thing is distinguished from everything else differs from its quiddity, existence, and origination: each of those can be common to it and something else, unlike its own individuation. Thus we can truly say of a universal that it has a quiddity, is existent, or is one, but not that it is individuated, although the concepts *individuation* and *individuated* are themselves universal concepts applicable to many. Individuation and distinctness (*tamayyuz*) overlap without being coextensive. Both apply to individual particularizations when the individuals are considered to share a quiddity: each is particular in itself and distinct from the others. Individuation without this comparative distinctness is predicated when shared quiddity is not taken into account; distinctness without individuation is predicated of universals—for example species differentiated from one another against their participation in a genus.

**Second investigation: the doctrine that individuation is considerational (*iʿtibārī*), not an externally actual existent.** Two arguments are offered. First, if individuation existed externally it would necessarily have an individuation of its own, and the argument would recur to infinity. **Objection:** the need for another individualizing feature follows only if individuations share a common quiddity and thus need differentiation. But perhaps their essences differ intrinsically, so that they share only the word *individuation* or the accidental concept it expresses. **Reply:** every existent has a universal quiddity in the intellect even if more than one individual instance is impossible in external reality. There are difficulties when this is asserted of the Necessary Existent; the argument is accordingly restricted to individuations, although the same objection continues to threaten it.

**Objection:** why could an individuation not be individuated through itself, preventing an infinite regress? **Reply:** the quiddity of individuation is universal. Its distinctness comes from particular features incapable of being shared, and the distinction between a subject and the feature inhering in it is necessary where both are externally real. Such identity is acceptable only with considerational objects, as when one speaks of the eternity of eternity or the origination of origination.

A second argument for individuation's considerational character is this: were it an externally existing attribute, its inherence in **this portion of a species** rather than another would presuppose the portion's external existence and its prior differentiation. If the differentiation resulted from the very individuation in question, a circle would follow; if from another individuation, a regress. This is what is intended by saying that an individuation's combination with the quiddity would presuppose the latter's distinctness. It cannot be answered merely that the quiddity is distinguished by its own essence and its differentiae, not by the individuation in question.

**Objection:** the subject of individuation could be precisely the portion differentiated by this same attribute, not by an antecedent attribute. The parallel is the **white body**, whose subject is the body that is white by this very whiteness, not by a prior whiteness. This is at most reciprocal simultaneity, not a vicious circle. Likewise a quiddity exists already specified by its individuating attributes, as portions of a genus are differentiated by specific differentiae. The attachment of a differentia does not presuppose another discrimination of its portion. **Reply:** a subject necessarily precedes its attribute in existence; hence its distinctness, accompanying the antecedent existence, must likewise precede the attribute. Generic portions differentiated by differentiae are different because their differentiation is merely intellectual. **Consideration:** the subject's priority to its individuation is priority **in essence**, not time. This does not imply that a concomitant of the subject also precedes it in time: something can depend on a thing without its own concomitant depending on that thing in the same fashion. **Further objection:** the allegedly antecedent subject is this very portion; that already presupposes its thisness (*hādhiyya*), namely individuation and distinction. **Reply:** calling it this portion means only that it is the subject of thisness; the thisness itself may result from the individuation under discussion.

Those who maintain individuation to be **real and existent** offer five arguments.

**(1)** Individuation is a constituent of the individuated, for an individuated thing is the combination of quiddity and individuation. The individual exists, and a constituent of an existent must exist. **Reply:** if *the individuated* means what is qualified by individuation, the latter is an accident of the former rather than one of its essential parts. If it means the aggregate of them both, it is not conceded that this aggregate has separate external actuality. Even when a qualification is sensible—as when a body is white—body-plus-whiteness is an aggregate constituted by the intellect. The argument is weaker still when the reality of the alleged qualifying feature is precisely what is disputed. The author of *al-Mawāqif* objects that the **individual person**, Zayd, indisputably exists. His concept is not simply *human*, or it would apply also to ʿAmr; rather it is human-plus-something called individuation, an existing constituent of Zayd. **Answer:** granted that Zayd's concept is not the bare universal *human*, why cannot it be *human qualified by definite individuating accidents*, rather than a composite aggregate? Even if an aggregate were conceded, a constituent of its **concept** need not exist separately outside the mind. And if we grant still more, that additional thing can be the individual's magnitude, qualities, filiation, and similar peculiarities, most of which are sensible and certainly existent. The opponents call these **that by which individuation obtains**, not individuation itself.

**(2)** A specific nature, such as humanity, does not of itself multiply: quiddity as such entails neither unity nor plurality. Its multiplication occurs through the addition of particular existing accidents, sometimes sensible ones; and this is what is meant by individuation.

**(3)** If individuation were privative, it would not itself be determinate, since what does not exist has no individually established identity; hence it could not determine something else. A thing without external establishment cannot be the cause of one entity's external distinction from all others. **Reply to (2) and (3):** it is agreed that particularizing accidents which attach to and multiply the nature do exist. That agreement does not settle whether a further supposed *individuation* over and above them exists.

**(4)** If individuation is privative, but not a merely absolute nothing, it must be the absence of **nonindividuation in general** or the absence of a particular individuation. That individuation will itself be privative or positive. On every option, the original individuation must be positive: on the first two, because the contradictory of a privative is positive; on the third, because similar things must be governed by the same rule. **Reply:** an item's being privative need not mean that it is the *absence of some specified positive item*; it may simply lack external existence, as we maintain of considerational things. Even if that premise is granted, the contradictory of a privative need not be externally positive: witness blindness and nonblindness. Moreover, if *individuation* and *nonindividuation* denote concepts, the proposed disjunction is not exhaustive; individuation could be the absence of some other concept. If they denote what falls under the concepts, it is not admitted that everything falling under nonindividuation is privative; nonindividuation may be said of any general reality. Finally, individuations need not be mutually alike in their essence: they may differ in kind while sharing the accidental concept *individuation*.

**(5)** If individuation is a privation, it must be the absence of something incompatible with it, such as absoluteness or unrestrictedness (*iṭlāq*), universality, or generality. If it is the absence of unrestrictedness—or of a condition whose absence cannot be separated from the absence of unrestrictedness—then it belongs equally to all individuals, since all individuals lack unrestrictedness. It will consequently not distinguish them, and so will not be individuation. But if it is not the absence of unrestrictedness or any such inseparable condition, the absence of unrestrictedness can be separated from the alleged privation. Either there is a lack of unrestrictedness **without** individuation, so that a thing is neither unrestricted nor individuated, violating the law of excluded middle; or individuation occurs **without** the lack of unrestrictedness, so that something is both unrestricted and individuated, combining contradictories. **Reply:** if the privation of unrestrictedness is said to constitute *individuation in general*, we deny that such a general concept cannot be shared by individuals: individuality belongs to each under its own **particular** individuation. If what is meant is *this particular individuation*, we choose the second alternative. It is the absence of something other than unrestrictedness, and other than any attribute whose absence is inseparable from the absence of unrestrictedness. One can have the absence of unrestrictedness without **this** particular individuation, and it follows only that a thing is neither unrestricted nor individuated **in this specific way**. It may be individuated in another, and no contradiction follows.

**Concluding caution.** Conceiving something in some respect may suffice for making a judgment about it in general; but **particular judgments may require a correspondingly determinate conception of their subject and predicate**. Before deciding whether individuation is positive or privative, considerational or nonconsiderational, the intended meanings of these predicates have to be specified.

title: Thisness, intelligible universals, philosophers' accounts of particularization, and modality
en:
To clarify the issue, a specific reality that is constituted through itself or through its essential constituents may acquire multiplicity through added quantities, qualities, positions, relations, different materials, and similar attributes. These may culminate in **thisness**, or the impossibility of sharing—as with *this* person or *that*—and are called **individuating accidents**. Before judging a proposition concerning individuation, we must determine whether its subject means those accidents themselves, the thisness resulting upon their presence, the impossibility of sharing, a portion of the species considered under such qualification, or something else. We must also establish the predicate: what are *positive*, *privative*, and *considerational*?

Some call **privative** whatever is nonexistent, others an absolute or relative privation, which may be composite with a positive item, as blindness is the absence of sight in a subject naturally apt for sight, or noncomposite, as incapacity for participation. Another account calls privative whatever has negation within its very concept—for instance being such that sharing is impossible. Correspondingly, *positive* can mean what exists, absolute or relative existence, or a concept without negation as a constituent. Meanings, not merely verbal forms, decide: blindness is privative, whereas non-nonexistence is positive. In *al-Mawāqif*, a **positive** description is one which, when attributed to a subject, is established for it by an external occurrence, as blackness is, not merely because subject and description are present and conjoined **in the intellect** as is possible with possibility. The category is wider than what actually exists, since something may be positive in meaning even if it never occurs. Al-Qāḍī al-Urmawī similarly says that calling something *positive* does not imply its continuous existence, only that it could acquire external existence when instantiated in an existent, while not existing when posited of a nonexistent. The intended range may be broader in one direction and narrower in another, for some actually existent items—such as a human, or other independently conceived notions—are not commonly called *positive descriptions* in this special sense. The **considerational** is what has no independent actuality outside the intellect's positing even when its subject possesses the description in reality itself (*nafs al-amr*). Thus a human is really *possible*, meaning that when the intellect relates human quiddity to existence it conceives the description *possibility*. Its contrary here is *real*. On these distinctions, the individuating accidents are positive; *thisness* is considerational; exclusion of every other individual, the impossibility of being shared, and being not-another are privative.

**Third investigation: a universal attached to another universal cannot by itself make a particular.** Individuation requires that the intellect cannot suppose the concept to be truly predicated of many. Combining universal with universal cannot ensure this: the thing combined, its qualifier, and the combination itself are each conceivable of indefinitely many subjects, even where external multiplication is impossible, as in the concept of the Necessary. **Objection:** a whole can have a property different from either constituent; why cannot two universal concepts form a particular whole? **Reply:** the alleged combination here means simply conceiving a universal, *human*, with another universal feature, *learned*. Such a qualified universal cannot reach *thisness*, even if one takes *particular*, *individuated*, or *incapable of sharing* as its additional predicates. A weaker reply observes that universal-plus-universal does not **necessitate** particularity even if in some instances it might produce it. But that conclusion is exceedingly obvious: *extended substance*, *growing body*, *rational animal*, and *learned human* may all still be universals; it hardly deserves demonstration as a scholarly thesis.

**Objection:** if universal qualification cannot individuate, the qualifying item that succeeds must be particular, and its own concept will be universal, again requiring a qualifier, and so on without end. **Reply:** there is not one independently existing universal and a second thing joining it to create a particular. What externally exist are **individuals**; from them the intellect abstracts universal forms under different dispositions and considerations. The contention is that no combination of universals is what removes the capacity for multiple application. According to us, the individualization of possible things rests on the **free and powerful agent**, who creates each instance with the particularity He wills.

Others attribute individuation to the quiddity's **coming to exist externally**: once it actually exists, it must be a definite individual with no further shared or multiple identity. Only the intellectual concept is open to repeated instantiation. **Objection:** if existence is one, individualization must likewise be one. **Reply:** existence is one in **concept**, not in individual instances. Its particulars vary with times, places, materials, and the other relevant causes, and the resulting individuations vary accordingly. **Further objection:** mere concomitance does not establish causality; external existence may be accompanied by individuating identity without being its productive ground. **Reply:** it is conceded that we recognize individuation whenever external existence is established, without needing separately to examine other features. But not examining something does not establish its absence. Actual existence presupposes a quiddity and effective or material causes or some ground on which that existence depends. Particularity may depend on that same ground. In any case, existence at most entails **some** individuation; what requires explanation is **this particular** individuation rather than another.

The philosophers maintain that individuation can be due to **quiddity itself or its concomitants**, as with the Necessary, whose quiddity can have only a single instance. If two instances of the same such quiddity were alleged, its effect would be present in one but absent in the other despite the same cause. In other cases individuation depends on something other than the quiddity. It cannot be **a thing completely separate from the individual**, since its relation to all individuals and individuations would be equal. It cannot be an **accident inhering in the individual**, since an accident's dependence on its subject makes it posterior to that subject, while its allegedly constituting individuation makes it prior to the very subject it individualizes: a contradiction. It must therefore have a subject in which the individual is situated, or a **receptacle** for the individual. Strictly, by the person's receptacle they mean the subject of an accident; the matter of a body; or the object of connection of a soul, given their teaching that the soul comes to exist after the body and is specified by its relation to it.

Consequently, each separate intellect, being free of matter, is individuated through its own quiddity and is singular within its type, not through a mere external relation such as *intellect of the first sphere*. Such a relation is posterior to the sphere, the sphere to the intellect, and the intellect's existent identity to its individuation. Matter grounds the individuation of bodily instances either immediately or through accidents inhering in it. This answers an objection that there are modes of individuation other than either an accident of the individual or a subject **for** it, since the accident could inhere in the subject of the individual instead. **Objection:** matter itself must be individuated. If through its quiddity, it cannot multiply; if through the particularization of the composite, the circle returns; and if through a further matter, the regress returns. **Reply:** by quantities, qualities, positions, and other successive accidents arising in matter through successive aptitudes. An infinite succession of noncontemporaneous such conditions is not, on their view, impossible; celestial movements and positions serve as their analogue. When individuation depends on matter, instances multiply with the multiplication of matter. Matter is intrinsically receptive of multiplicity; it need not possess an additional receptacle, although it requires an agent to multiply it.

**Objection:** if the accidents that inhere in matter become particular only through the prior particularity of matter, matter cannot itself be particularized by them. **Reply:** matter is particularized by **the accidents themselves** insofar as they occur in it, not by the accidents' own particularities resulting from matter's prior particularity. Their individuality is through matter, while matter's is with their occurrence, so neither a vicious circle nor a particular produced through the combination of universals is implied. Yet the reply makes a further difficulty acute: if this sort of account works, why cannot a quiddity's instances multiply and be individualized simply through the various attributes attaching to them, **without requiring matter**?

**Second approach (*manhaj*): necessity, impossibility, and possibility.** Impossibility is included among the concomitants of existence and quiddity because necessity of the negation of existence is a state of the two; or because impossibility qualifies a quiddity as understood; or because it stands opposite possibility; or simply because these are topics customarily treated after existence and quiddity.

**First investigation.** In logical inquiry the question *Is it?* (*hal*) is either **simple**, asking whether a thing exists in itself, or **composite**, asking whether an attribute exists for a thing. Relating a concept to its existence in itself, or the existence of a predicate for it, yields the three notions **necessity (*wujūb*)**, **impossibility (*imtināʿ*)**, and **possibility (*imkān*)**. The predication of existence, or the bond between subject and predicate, can be necessary: *The Exalted Creator exists*, *four is even*. To clarify the issue, a specific reality that is constituted through itself or through its essential constituents may acquire multiplicity through added quantities, qualities, positions, relations, different materials, and similar attributes. These may culminate in thisness, or the impossibility of sharing—as with this person or that—and are called individuating accidents. Before judging a proposition concerning individuation, we must determine whether its subject means those accidents themselves, the thisness resulting upon their presence, the impossibility of sharing, a portion of the species considered under such qualification, or something else. We must also establish the predicate: what are positive, privative, and considerational?

Some call privative whatever is nonexistent, others an absolute or relative privation, which may be composite with a positive item, as blindness is the absence of sight in a subject naturally apt for sight, or noncomposite, as incapacity for participation. Another account calls privative whatever has negation within its very concept—for instance being such that sharing is impossible. Correspondingly, positive can mean what exists, absolute or relative existence, or a concept without negation as a constituent. Meanings, not merely verbal forms, decide: blindness is privative, whereas non-nonexistence is positive. In al-Mawāqif, a positive description is one which, when attributed to a subject, is established for it by an external occurrence, as blackness is, not merely because subject and description are present and conjoined in the intellect as is possible with possibility. The category is wider than what actually exists, since something may be positive in meaning even if it never occurs. Al-Qāḍī al-Urmawī similarly says that calling something positive does not imply its continuous existence, only that it could acquire external existence when instantiated in an existent, while not existing when posited of a nonexistent. The intended range may be broader in one direction and narrower in another, for some actually existent items—such as a human, or other independently conceived notions—are not commonly called positive descriptions in this special sense. The considerational is what has no independent actuality outside the intellect's positing even when its subject possesses the description in reality itself (nafs al-amr). Thus a human is really possible, meaning that when the intellect relates human quiddity to existence it conceives the description possibility. Its contrary here is real. On these distinctions, the individuating accidents are positive; thisness is considerational; exclusion of every other individual, the impossibility of being shared, and being not-another are privative.

Third investigation: a universal attached to another universal cannot by itself make a particular. Individuation requires that the intellect cannot suppose the concept to be truly predicated of many. Combining universal with universal cannot ensure this: the thing combined, its qualifier, and the combination itself are each conceivable of indefinitely many subjects, even where external multiplication is impossible, as in the concept of the Necessary. Objection: a whole can have a property different from either constituent; why cannot two universal concepts form a particular whole? Reply: the alleged combination here means simply conceiving a universal, human, with another universal feature, learned. Such a qualified universal cannot reach thisness, even if one takes particular, individuated, or incapable of sharing as its additional predicates. A weaker reply observes that universal-plus-universal does not necessitate particularity even if in some instances it might produce it. But that conclusion is exceedingly obvious: extended substance, growing body, rational animal, and learned human may all still be universals; it hardly deserves demonstration as a scholarly thesis.

Objection: if universal qualification cannot individuate, the qualifying item that succeeds must be particular, and its own concept will be universal, again requiring a qualifier, and so on without end. Reply: there is not one independently existing universal and a second thing joining it to create a particular. What externally exist are individuals; from them the intellect abstracts universal forms under different dispositions and considerations. The contention is that no combination of universals is what removes the capacity for multiple application. According to us, the individualization of possible things rests on the free and powerful agent, who creates each instance with the particularity He wills.

Others attribute individuation to the quiddity's coming to exist externally: once it actually exists, it must be a definite individual with no further shared or multiple identity. Only the intellectual concept is open to repeated instantiation. Objection: if existence is one, individualization must likewise be one. Reply: existence is one in concept, not in individual instances. Its particulars vary with times, places, materials, and the other relevant causes, and the resulting individuations vary accordingly. Further objection: mere concomitance does not establish causality; external existence may be accompanied by individuating identity without being its productive ground. Reply: it is conceded that we recognize individuation whenever external existence is established, without needing separately to examine other features. But not examining something does not establish its absence. Actual existence presupposes a quiddity and effective or material causes or some ground on which that existence depends. Particularity may depend on that same ground. In any case, existence at most entails some individuation; what requires explanation is this particular individuation rather than another.

The philosophers maintain that individuation can be due to quiddity itself or its concomitants, as with the Necessary, whose quiddity can have only a single instance. If two instances of the same such quiddity were alleged, its effect would be present in one but absent in the other despite the same cause. In other cases individuation depends on something other than the quiddity. It cannot be a thing completely separate from the individual, since its relation to all individuals and individuations would be equal. It cannot be an accident inhering in the individual, since an accident's dependence on its subject makes it posterior to that subject, while its allegedly constituting individuation makes it prior to the very subject it individualizes: a contradiction. It must therefore have a subject in which the individual is situated, or a receptacle for the individual. Strictly, by the person's receptacle they mean the subject of an accident; the matter of a body; or the object of connection of a soul, given their teaching that the soul comes to exist after the body and is specified by its relation to it.

Consequently, each separate intellect, being free of matter, is individuated through its own quiddity and is singular within its type, not through a mere external relation such as intellect of the first sphere. Such a relation is posterior to the sphere, the sphere to the intellect, and the intellect's existent identity to its individuation. Matter grounds the individuation of bodily instances either immediately or through accidents inhering in it. This answers an objection that there are modes of individuation other than either an accident of the individual or a subject for it, since the accident could inhere in the subject of the individual instead. An infinite succession of noncontemporaneous such conditions is not, on their view, impossible; celestial movements and positions serve as their analogue. Matter is intrinsically receptive of multiplicity; it need not possess an additional receptacle, although it requires an agent to multiply it.
